text: Diabetic retinopathy is damage to the small blood vessels of the retina caused by long-standing high blood sugar in people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. It is one of the most common causes of preventable sight loss in working-age adults.

Diabetic retinopathy is graded on a five-point scale: 0 no retinopathy; 1 mild non-proliferative (microaneurysms only); 2 moderate non-proliferative; 3 severe non-proliferative; 4 proliferative retinopathy with new abnormal blood vessels.

A grade of 'no diabetic retinopathy' means no visible retinal changes were detected. People with diabetes should still attend routine eye screening, usually once a year, because retinopathy can develop between visits.

Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy means only microaneurysms (tiny bulges in retinal capillaries) are present. Vision is usually unaffected. Management is tighter control of blood glucose, blood pressure and cholesterol, with continued annual or more frequent screening.

Moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy shows microaneurysms together with dot-and-blot haemorrhages and often hard exudates. It is generally considered referable disease: the patient should be seen by an ophthalmologist for assessment and closer follow-up.

Severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy involves extensive haemorrhages in all four retinal quadrants, venous beading, or intraretinal microvascular abnormalities. It carries a high risk of progressing to proliferative disease and needs prompt ophthalmology referral.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is the advanced stage, defined by neovascularisation (growth of fragile new vessels) and/or vitreous or pre-retinal haemorrhage. It threatens sight and requires urgent, sometimes emergency, ophthalmology assessment and treatment.

In most screening programmes, 'referable diabetic retinopathy' means moderate non-proliferative disease or worse (grade 2 and above), or any diabetic maculopathy. Grades 0 and 1 are usually managed by routine re-screening rather than referral.

Referral urgency rises with severity: moderate retinopathy is a routine ophthalmology referral, severe non-proliferative retinopathy is a prompt referral, and proliferative retinopathy or sight-threatening maculopathy is an urgent or emergency referral.

Early diabetic retinopathy usually has no symptoms, which is why screening is essential. Later symptoms can include blurred or fluctuating vision, dark floaters or streaks, patchy vision loss, and difficulty seeing at night.

The main risk factors for developing and progressing diabetic retinopathy are longer duration of diabetes, poor blood glucose control (high HbA1c), high blood pressure, high blood lipids, kidney disease, and pregnancy.

Randomised trials show that intensive control of blood glucose substantially reduces the risk of diabetic retinopathy developing and slows its progression; good blood pressure control adds further benefit.

Adults with diabetes and no retinopathy are typically screened every one to two years. Screening is more frequent when retinopathy is present, when diabetes control is poor, and during pregnancy, when progression can be rapid.
Pregnancy can accelerate diabetic retinopathy. Women with pre-existing diabetes are advised to have an eye assessment before or early in pregnancy and further checks during each trimester as needed.

Treatments for sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy include laser photocoagulation (including pan-retinal laser for proliferative disease), intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (especially for diabetic macular oedema), intravitreal steroids in selected cases, and vitrectomy surgery for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment.

Diabetic maculopathy (including diabetic macular oedema) is fluid leakage and thickening at the macula, the part of the retina responsible for central vision. It can occur at any retinopathy stage and is a common cause of vision loss in diabetes.

Screening programmes use colour fundus photography: a specialised camera photographs the back of the eye, often after dilating drops, and the images are graded by trained readers or, increasingly, by validated software.

Automated retinopathy grading tools are decision-support aids, not a replacement for an eye examination. They can miss or misclassify disease, perform worse on poor-quality images, and are usually validated only on specific populations and cameras. A clinician makes the final decision.

Anyone with diabetes who notices sudden vision loss, a shower of new floaters, flashing lights, a dark curtain across vision, or eye pain should seek same-day medical attention regardless of their last screening result.

With timely screening and treatment, severe vision loss from diabetic retinopathy is largely preventable. Most sight loss occurs when disease is detected late or follow-up is missed, so keeping screening appointments matters even when vision seems normal.
